lessons.title: Measuring Global Inequalities
lessons.description: GNI, GDP and why a single number can never tell the full story of global development.
lessons.content_html:
What is Development?

Development describes how a country becomes ‘better off’ for its citizens — not just richer, but healthier, better educated, better governed and more equal. Geographers measure development to compare countries, track progress over time and direct aid where it is most needed. The challenge is that development has many faces, and any single number captures only part of the picture. Eduqas Theme 6 starts with this puzzle: how do we measure something so complex without losing the detail?

Key Fact

The two most common economic measures are GNI (Gross National Income) and GDP (Gross Domestic Product). Both express national wealth in US dollars per person, but neither tells you how wealth is shared, how long people live or how many can read.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP)

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of goods and services made within a country’s borders in a year. Divide by population and you get GDP per capita, which lets you compare countries of different sizes. The UK’s GDP per capita in 2024 sat at around US$48,000; Bangladesh’s at about US$2,600; the United States at about US$80,000. GDP captures economic output well but ignores anything happening outside markets — unpaid care work, subsistence farming, environmental damage — so a country with rapid GDP growth can still be polluting its rivers and overworking its citizens.

Gross National Income (GNI)

Gross National Income (GNI) — the headline measure used by Eduqas — is broader than GDP. It counts everything earned by a country’s residents, including profits and wages flowing in from overseas. For countries with lots of citizens working abroad (such as the Philippines, where remittances were about US$38 billion in 2023, equal to 9% of GDP), GNI is meaningfully larger than GDP. The World Bank uses GNI per capita to classify countries: low-income (under US$1,145), lower-middle, upper-middle and high-income (over US$14,005 in 2024).

Total GDP can be misleading. China’s GDP (about US$18 trillion in 2024) is roughly six times the UK’s — but China has 21 times more people. Per-capita figures (GDP / population) flip the comparison: UK GDP per capita is about US$48,000 versus China’s US$13,000. China is the world’s second-largest economy in total terms and a middle-income country in per-person terms. Both stories are true, and Eduqas examiners want students who can see both at once.

Limitations of Single Numbers

Wealth measures hide three big problems. Inequality: GNI per capita is an average. South Africa’s upper-middle income status conceals one of the world’s widest wealth gaps — the richest 10% earn 65% of national income. Informal economies: in much of sub-Saharan Africa, around 85% of jobs are informal (street markets, smallholder farming, casual labour) and are missed from GDP entirely. Quality of life: numbers say nothing about life expectancy, schooling, freedom or safety. Cuba’s GNI per capita is only US$9,500 but Cubans live to 79 on average — longer than far richer countries. To capture these, geographers use composite measures alongside money.

Composite Measures & the Development Continuum

The Human Development Index (HDI) combines GNI per capita, life expectancy and average years of schooling into a single 0-to-1 score. Norway sits near the top at 0.97; the UK at 0.94; India at 0.64; South Sudan near the bottom at 0.39. Other useful measures include literacy rates, doctors per 1,000 people, infant mortality and access to safe water. Together, these data points form a development continuum — a sliding scale, not a binary split. The simple ‘rich North, poor South’ map of the 1980s no longer fits a world where China, India and Brazil are catching up fast.

The development gap is the difference in living standards between richer and poorer countries. It is dynamic: in 1990, China’s GNI per capita was less than 5% of the UK’s; by 2024 it was around 25%. Vietnam moved from low-income to lower-middle income within thirty years. But other countries have stalled: South Sudan’s HDI has barely moved since 2011 because of conflict. The gap is closing in some places and widening in others — one reason geographers prefer the continuum to the old binary classification.

Key Fact

GDP per capita is a useful starting point but masks inequality (averages hide gaps), excludes informal economies (a huge share of work in many LICs), and ignores life expectancy, schooling and well-being. Reliable development analysis pairs an income measure with a composite measure such as HDI.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 3-mark explain questions, link the cause (e.g. inequality) to the effect on the data (e.g. high GNI per capita can hide most people living on much less). For 4-mark compare questions, examiners want explicit linking words — ‘whereas’, ‘in contrast’, ‘similarly’. For 6-mark named-example questions, give a country with at least one number (UK, Bangladesh, China, South Africa). For 8-mark evaluations, weigh the strengths and weaknesses of single-figure measures before reaching a judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • GDP and GNI per capita measure economic output and income, but ignore inequality, the informal economy and quality of life.
  • Composite measures like HDI combine income, life expectancy and schooling for a fuller picture — HDI runs from 0 (worst) to 1 (best).
  • The development gap is dynamic: countries spread along a continuum and individual countries can move up (China, Vietnam) or stall (South Sudan) over time.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes GNI per capita?
A) Total goods and services produced inside a country
B) Total income earned by a country's residents (including from abroad), divided by population
C) Average life expectancy at birth
D) The percentage of adults who can read
practice_questions.marks: B) Total income earned by a country's residents (including from abroad), divided by population [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Human Development Index (HDI) measures.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for a developed description:
• A composite measure that combines GNI per capita, life expectancy and average years of schooling into a single score (1).
• Each country is given a value from 0 (lowest development) to 1 (highest), allowing fair comparison across regions (1).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why GDP per capita can be a misleading measure of development.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a developed cause-effect chain:
• GDP per capita is an average that hides inequality — a small wealthy elite can pull the figure up while most people live in poverty (e.g. South Africa) (1).
• Much economic activity in lower-income countries happens in the informal sector and is not counted, so GDP underestimates real economic activity (1).
• It says nothing about life expectancy, education or quality of life — Cuba's GDP is low but life expectancy is around 79 years (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare GNI per capita and HDI as measures of development.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit explicit comparison words:
• GNI per capita is a single economic figure measuring income, whereas HDI is a composite of income, education and health (1).
• GNI per capita is easier to calculate and update annually, in contrast HDI requires more data and lags behind (1).
• Both rank countries on a sliding scale, similarly placing them along a development continuum (1).
• HDI better reflects quality of life, whereas GNI better reflects raw economic power (1).
[4 marks — must include explicit comparison links]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how the development gap between two countries can be measured.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a developed answer with named countries and figures:
• Names two countries at different points on the continuum, e.g. UK and Bangladesh (1).
• Provides GNI per capita figures: UK around US$48,000, Bangladesh around US$2,600 in 2024 (1).
• Adds HDI scores: UK 0.94, Bangladesh 0.66 (1).
• Includes life expectancy: UK 81 years, Bangladesh 73 years (1).
• Identifies one further measure such as years of schooling or infant mortality (1).
• Concludes by recognising the gap is closing but remains substantial across multiple measures (1).
[6 marks — locational detail and named figures are essential]

practice_questions.text:
'A single economic figure such as GNI per capita is the best way to measure global development.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Use the StudyVault rubric.

Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing GNI's strengths (clarity, comparability, World Bank classifications) against its weaknesses (inequality, informal economy, quality of life). Uses named country examples (Cuba, South Africa, China) with figures. Reaches a justified conclusion (e.g. GNI is necessary but not sufficient — must be paired with HDI or other measures).

Secure: Clear arguments for and against. Some named examples and figures. Conclusion partly asserted.

Developing: Some arguments on each side; examples generic ('a rich country', 'a poor country'). Limited weighing.

Emerging: Simple comments on GNI with no comparison and no examples.

In favour: GNI is updated annually, internationally consistent, easy to compare; underpins World Bank country categories; correlates strongly with most other indicators.
Against: hides inequality (South Africa); ignores informal sector (sub-Saharan Africa, ~85% informal); says nothing about life expectancy (Cuba); can mask environmental damage from rapid growth; should be paired with HDI to be useful.
[8 marks]

lessons.title: Causes of Uneven Development
lessons.description: How trade rules, multinationals and tourism create uneven development between richer and poorer countries.
lessons.content_html:
Why Are Some Countries Richer Than Others?

Development is uneven across the world, and the causes are rarely just bad luck. Three forces shape today’s pattern: the rules of global trade, the choices of multinational companies (MNCs), and the spread of international tourism. Each force creates winners and losers — and rarely splits them evenly between high-income countries (HICs), newly industrialised countries (NICs) and low-income countries (LICs).

Key Fact

The three main drivers of uneven development at the global scale are international trade, multinational companies and tourism. All three connect richer and poorer countries but do so on unequal terms.

Trade and the Rules of the Game

Countries grow richer when they sell more than they buy. Exports bring money in; imports take it out. Many LICs export primary products — cocoa, coffee, copper, oil — whose prices swing wildly on world markets. HICs and NICs export manufactured goods and services, which earn far higher and steadier prices. A tonne of raw cocoa earns Ghanaian farmers a fraction of what Swiss chocolate makers earn from the same beans turned into bars.

The rules of trade can deepen this gap. Trade blocs like the European Union remove tariffs between members but charge them on imports from outside. Tariffs, quotas (limits on how much can be imported) and subsidies (government payments to a country’s own farmers or producers) all tilt the playing field. EU sugar subsidies, for example, made it cheaper for African producers to sell cane sugar to Europe than for Europeans to buy it — until the subsidies were reformed.

Around 60% of Zambia’s export earnings still come from copper. When the world copper price falls, Zambia’s government has less tax income for schools, roads and hospitals overnight. A country that exports a wider range of finished goods — cars, electronics, clothing — spreads its risk. This is one reason China and Vietnam climbed faster up the development continuum than Zambia or Burkina Faso: they shifted from raw exports into manufacturing.

Multinational Companies

An MNC has its head office in one country and factories, offices or shops in many others. Apple is American, but its iPhones are assembled in China and Vietnam from parts made in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan. MNCs locate plants where labour is cheaper, taxes are lower or raw materials sit close by. The biggest MNCs, like Walmart or Toyota, earn more than the GNI of most LICs.

For host LICs and NICs, MNCs bring real benefits: jobs, training, technology, infrastructure and tax revenue. The clothing industry helped lift millions of Bangladeshi women out of household poverty. But the costs are real too. Wages are often low, working conditions can be harsh, profits flow back to the home country and MNCs may leave when costs rise — closing factories overnight. The 2013 collapse of the Rana Plaza garment factory in Dhaka, which killed over 1,100 workers, became a symbol of these trade-offs.

Key Fact

MNCs bring jobs, infrastructure and technology to host countries but often pay low wages, repatriate profits and can relocate suddenly. The balance depends on the strength of the host government and labour laws.

Tourism as a Development Driver

Tourism is now one of the world’s biggest industries, and many LICs and NICs treat it as a fast track to growth. Cheaper flights, the internet and rising HIC incomes mean places like Kenya, Thailand and the Maldives now host millions of international visitors a year. Tourism creates jobs in hotels, transport, food, guiding and crafts, and it brings in foreign currency that can be spent on schools and hospitals.

But tourist money does not always stay where it is spent. Enclave tourism — where visitors stay inside a foreign-owned resort, eat imported food and book through an HIC travel firm — can mean as little as 20% of the price they pay reaches the local economy. Cultural impacts add to the picture: traditional ways of life can become a performance for tourists, and rising prices push locals out of their own neighbourhoods.

Tourism contributes around 10% of Kenya’s GDP and supports more than a million jobs around the Maasai Mara safari parks and Mombasa coast. New airports, roads and water supplies follow. Yet many resorts are foreign-owned, terrorist attacks and political unrest can collapse bookings overnight, and Maasai communities have lost grazing land to private game reserves. The challenge is to spread tourism’s gains while protecting the people and wildlife that draw visitors in the first place.

Putting the Pieces Together

Trade rules, MNCs and tourism are not separate stories — they reinforce each other. An MNC opens a textile factory in Bangladesh because trade rules favour exporting clothes to Europe. A trade bloc lowers air-fare taxes, so tourists fly to Kenya instead of holidaying at home. Each decision in a head office in London, Tokyo or New York reshapes opportunities in Lusaka, Hanoi or Mumbai. The development gap is not natural — it is built and rebuilt every day by these connections.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 6-mark ‘Explain with Example’ question on uneven development, name a specific country and a specific industry — ‘Bangladesh’s garment industry employs four million people, mostly women’ scores far higher than ‘in some LICs’. For 8-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions, weigh the benefits of MNCs or tourism against the costs and reach a clear judgement, e.g. ‘On balance, MNCs accelerate development when host governments enforce strong labour laws.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Uneven global development is driven by trade rules (tariffs, quotas, subsidies, primary-product dependence), MNC location decisions and the rise of international tourism.
  • MNCs bring jobs, technology and infrastructure but often pay low wages, send profits home and can relocate suddenly — the host country’s laws shape the balance.
  • Tourism boosts GDP and employment in countries like Kenya, but enclave resorts and cultural change can limit how much benefit reaches local communities.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a tariff?
A) A government payment given to local farmers
B) A tax placed on goods imported from another country
C) A limit on how many goods can be imported
D) A free-trade agreement between countries
practice_questions.marks: B) A tax placed on goods imported from another country [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of enclave tourism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear feature with brief development, e.g. visitors stay inside a self-contained resort owned by a foreign company, so little of what they spend reaches the local economy. Secure: feature identified with limited development. Developing: vague reference to tourism only benefiting some people. Emerging: no feature identified or definition restated.

practice_questions.text: Explain how trade rules can hold back development in LICs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear cause-and-effect chain with two examples — tariffs raise the price of LIC exports in HIC markets, reducing demand; subsidies make HIC products artificially cheap, undercutting LIC producers; quotas cap how much LICs can sell. Secure: one mechanism with effect. Developing: states trade is unfair without explanation. Emerging: no link to development.

practice_questions.text: Compare the impact of MNCs and tourism as drivers of development in lower-income countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words (similarly, whereas, in contrast) on at least two points — both create jobs, but MNC jobs are factory-based whereas tourism jobs are service-based; both bring foreign money in, however MNC profits often leave the country whereas tourism revenue can flow more directly into local services if non-enclave. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features of each separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how multinational companies have affected development in one named LIC or NIC. Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account with named country (e.g. Bangladesh, Vietnam, Mexico) and named MNC or industry (e.g. garment industry employing four million workers; Foxconn assembling Apple products in Vietnam) covering at least two impacts — jobs, training, infrastructure, tax revenue against low wages, profit repatriation, sudden closures. Secure: named country with two impacts but limited locational detail. Developing: generic LIC reference, one impact. Emerging: vague reference without named place.

practice_questions.text:
“Tourism does more harm than good for the development of LICs and NICs.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples (e.g. Kenya, Thailand, Maldives) weighing benefits (employment, foreign currency, infrastructure such as roads and airports, multiplier effects) against costs (enclave resorts limiting local income, cultural change, environmental pressure, vulnerability to political shocks) and reaching a justified judgement (e.g. tourism is a net positive when local ownership is encouraged but harmful when it stays in foreign-owned enclaves). Secure: balanced argument with one named example and a clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided argument or generic without named places. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

lessons.title: Responses to Uneven Development
lessons.description: How aid, NGOs and fair trade try to close the gap between richer and poorer countries.
lessons.content_html:
Closing the Development Gap

Uneven development is not inevitable. Governments, charities and international agreements have tried for decades to narrow the gap between richer and poorer countries. Three responses dominate: aid, the work of NGOs, and fair trade. Each works in a different way, and each has strengths and weaknesses.

Key Fact

The three main global responses to uneven development are international aid, the work of NGOs and the fair trade movement. They differ in scale, in who delivers them and in how long they last.

Types of Aid

Aid splits into two broad types. Emergency aid arrives quickly after a disaster — food, water, tents, medical teams. After the 2010 Haiti earthquake, the UN appealed for $1.5 billion to feed 3 million survivors. Long-term development aid is slower and steadier — it builds schools, clinics, wells and roads, and trains local people to run them.

Aid can flow in three ways. Bilateral aid goes from one government directly to another, sometimes with conditions attached such as buying products from the donor country. Multilateral aid is pooled through international bodies like the United Nations and World Bank and shared between many recipients. Voluntary aid is raised by the public for charities such as Oxfam or the Red Cross.

In 2015 the United Nations agreed 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to be reached by 2030. They include ending extreme poverty, ensuring all children complete primary school, and providing clean water and sanitation for all. The SDGs replaced the earlier Millennium Development Goals and act as a shared scoreboard for governments, NGOs and donors. Progress has been uneven — child mortality has fallen sharply, but climate change is now pushing some targets further out of reach.

Strengths and Weaknesses of Aid

Aid saves lives in emergencies and can transform schools, clinics and water supplies. But aid is also criticised. Large amounts can be lost to corruption before they reach the people who need them. Tied aid may force recipients to buy from the donor country, undermining local businesses. Some economists argue that decades of aid have left countries dependent rather than self-reliant. Others reply that without aid, life expectancy in many LICs would be far lower today.

Key Fact

Aid saves lives in emergencies and funds schools, clinics and water supplies. But it can be lost to corruption, tied to donor-country purchases and create dependency if not paired with local capacity-building.

NGOs — Working Closer to the Ground

NGOs include large international charities such as Oxfam, WaterAid, Save the Children and Médecins Sans Frontières, as well as thousands of small local organisations. Because they are not run by governments, NGOs can often work in remote villages or war zones where official aid agencies struggle. Their projects are usually small-scale: a hand-pump well for a village in Mali, a girls’ school in rural Bangladesh, training health workers in Sierra Leone.

NGO projects tend to favour bottom-up development — working with local communities to choose what they need rather than imposing top-down solutions from outside. WaterAid’s rope-pump wells in Malawi, for example, can be built and maintained by local people using parts available in the nearest market town. The technology is appropriate to local skills and budgets.

Fair Trade

Fair trade tackles the unfairness in global trade rather than relying on aid. Farmers and producers who join a fair trade scheme are guaranteed a fair, stable minimum price for their crop — for example, Fairtrade-certified cocoa farmers in Ghana receive at least US$2,400 per tonne, plus an extra premium of US$240 per tonne. The premium goes into a community fund that pays for schools, clinics or new equipment.

Fair trade products earn higher prices for farmers and have funded schools and water projects across coffee, cocoa and banana communities in Latin America and Africa. But critics argue the premium reaches only a small fraction of the world’s farmers, and certification fees can shut out the very poorest. Others worry it props up production of crops the world already has too much of. The most balanced view is that fair trade helps the farmers it reaches but cannot, on its own, fix global trade rules.

Putting Responses Together

No single response will close the development gap. Emergency aid keeps people alive after a hurricane; long-term aid and NGO projects build the schools, water systems and clinics that lift the next generation; fair trade pays farmers a price closer to what their work is worth. The countries that have moved up the development continuum most quickly — Vietnam, Bangladesh, Rwanda — have combined all three with their own government investment and sound policy.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark ‘Explain with Example’ questions, anchor every answer in a real organisation and a real place — ‘WaterAid’s rope-pump wells in Malawi’ beats ‘a charity in Africa’. For 8-mark evaluations, weigh strengths against weaknesses and reach a clear judgement; markers want to see ‘On balance...’ or ‘Overall, fair trade is most effective where...’ rather than a string of unjudged points.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Emergency aid tackles short-term crises while long-term development aid funds schools, clinics and water supplies; both can be bilateral, multilateral or voluntary.
  • NGOs often work bottom-up with local communities using appropriate technology, reaching villages where governments cannot, but they operate at smaller scale than official aid.
  • Fair trade pays producers in poorer countries a stable minimum price plus a community premium; it helps participating farmers but cannot, on its own, rewrite global trade rules.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines emergency aid?
A) Long-term aid that builds schools and clinics over many years
B) Short-term aid given immediately after a disaster
C) A loan from one government to another with conditions
D) The community premium paid to fair trade farmers
practice_questions.marks: B) Short-term aid given immediately after a disaster [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of long-term development aid.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear feature with brief development, e.g. it funds lasting projects such as schools, clinics, water supplies or training, building local capacity over many years. Secure: feature identified with limited development. Developing: vague reference to helping poor countries. Emerging: no feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain how fair trade benefits producers in low-income countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear chain — a guaranteed minimum price protects farmers from world price crashes; a community premium funds schools or clinics; producers gain a more stable income they can plan around. Secure: one mechanism with effect. Developing: states fair trade is good without explanation. Emerging: no link to producers.

practice_questions.text: Compare emergency aid and long-term development aid.

lessons.title: Water Resources & Management
lessons.description: Why water demand is rising fast and how dams, transfers and shared rivers manage the strain.
lessons.content_html:
A Thirstier World

Global water consumption has more than doubled since 1980. Three forces drive the rise: a growing world population, a richer global middle class eating more meat and dairy, and the spread of intensive farming. Geographers measure the pressure with two ideas. Water footprint tracks how much water sits behind everyday goods — one cotton T-shirt uses 2,700 litres; one beef burger uses 2,400 litres. Water security describes whether a country has enough safe water to meet its needs.

Key Fact

Global water demand is rising because the population is growing, diets are becoming more meat-heavy, and farming and industry are using more water per person. Water security is now a development issue, not just an environmental one.

Where the Water Goes

Worldwide, around 70% of fresh water is used for agriculture, 20% for industry and 10% for domestic uses such as drinking, washing and toilets. The mix shifts with development: HICs use a much bigger share for industry, while LICs lean heavily on agriculture. The poorest households can spend hours a day collecting water from distant pumps or rivers, time that would otherwise be spent at school or earning a living.

Big Reservoirs and Big Dams

When demand outgrows local supply, governments turn to large engineering projects. Reservoirs behind dams store winter rainfall for use in summer. The Three Gorges Dam on China’s Yangtze River is the world’s biggest hydropower project and supplies water and electricity to tens of millions. The Akosombo Dam on Ghana’s Volta River created Lake Volta, one of the world’s largest artificial lakes, and irrigates farmland across the south of the country.

Big dams bring real benefits — year-round water, flood control, hydro-electricity, irrigation. They also cause serious problems. The Three Gorges reservoir flooded 13 cities and 140 towns and forced 1.3 million people to move. Sediment that once fertilised downstream farms now collects behind the dam wall. Wildlife habitats are destroyed, and earthquake risk can rise where heavy water sits over old fault lines.

Not every solution needs a giant concrete wall. Rainwater harvesting — capturing runoff from roofs into household tanks — works well in places like rural India, where the monsoon delivers most of the year’s rain in a few months. NGOs help build community check-dams that slow streams and let water soak into the ground. These appropriate-technology projects are cheaper, easier to maintain and rarely displace anyone, although their scale is smaller than a national dam scheme.

Water Transfers

Some countries move water across the country to balance wet and dry regions. China’s South-North Water Transfer Project pipes water nearly 1,500 km from the wet Yangtze basin to the dry, populous north around Beijing. The UK transfers water from rainy upland Wales (Lake Vyrnwy) to the much drier Midlands. Transfers can be politically and environmentally controversial: source regions worry about losing their own water, and the energy needed to pump water uphill can be huge.

Groundwater — A Hidden Crisis

Groundwater abstraction draws water from underground aquifers using boreholes. In good times this is a stable, clean supply. In northern India and the south-western United States, however, farmers have pumped so heavily that water tables are falling several metres a year. Wells run dry. Land sinks. Saltwater can creep into coastal aquifers, ruining them for drinking. Aquifers can take centuries to refill, so over-abstraction is closer to mining than to renewable use.

Key Fact

Big dams provide year-round water, hydro-electricity and flood control but flood farmland and homes, displace large populations and trap sediment behind the wall. Sustainability depends on weighing these against local alternatives.

Shared Rivers and Politics

Almost half the world’s land sits in transboundary river basins, and managing them is a political challenge as much as a technical one. The Nile is shared by 11 countries; Egypt, near the river’s mouth, depends on it for 95% of its water. When Ethiopia began filling the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam upstream in 2020, Egypt and Sudan feared their flow would drop. Years of negotiation followed. The basic rule of transboundary rivers is that the actions of one country quickly become a problem for another.

A sustainable water future combines several strategies: efficient drip irrigation in farming (which can cut water use by half compared with flood irrigation), recycling treated wastewater for industry, rainwater harvesting in homes, repairing leaky pipes (London still loses around a fifth of its supply to leaks), and pricing water properly so heavy users pay more. Climate change adds urgency: warmer temperatures shrink mountain glaciers that feed rivers in summer, and rainfall is becoming less reliable. Water management is no longer about engineering alone — it is about choices.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark questions on water management, always anchor the answer in named places — ‘The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze displaced 1.3 million people’ beats ‘dams flood villages’. For 8-mark evaluations, weigh costs against benefits and reach a justified judgement; markers want a clear ‘On balance...’ statement, not a list of points.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Water demand is rising worldwide because of population growth, richer diets and industrial growth; water security is now central to development.
  • Large dams (e.g. Three Gorges, Akosombo) and water transfers (e.g. China’s South-North project) deliver supply at scale but flood land, displace people and trap sediment.
  • Groundwater abstraction is unsustainable when wells are pumped faster than aquifers refill, and shared rivers like the Nile turn water management into international politics.

lessons.title: UK Regional Inequalities
lessons.description: Why the UK has a north-south divide, and how multipliers and investment can help rebalance it.
lessons.content_html:
Two Speeds, One Country

Walk down a high street in Newcastle, then one in Reading, and you are in the same country at very different speeds. The UK has one of the widest regional gaps in Europe. The clearest pattern is the north-south divide: London and the south-east tend to be richer, healthier and better connected, while parts of the north of England, south Wales and the western edges of Scotland and Northern Ireland trail behind on average.

Key Fact

The UK’s north-south divide shows up in income, life expectancy, employment and house prices. London and the south-east lead on most measures, while parts of the north, south Wales and northern Scotland trail behind.

The Numbers Behind the Divide

The gap is real and measurable. Average GDP per person in inner London is more than double the figure for the north-east of England. Boys born in Blackpool today have a life expectancy nearly nine years lower than boys born in parts of west London. Unemployment, child poverty and the share of the population claiming benefits all skew north and west. House prices follow money: an average flat in London costs more than a four-bedroom house in much of the north.

Why the Divide Exists

The roots are partly historical. The 19th-century industrial revolution made northern cities like Manchester, Sheffield and Glasgow rich on coal, steel, shipbuilding and textiles. From the 1970s onwards those industries collapsed under foreign competition, leaving high unemployment and shrinking populations. London, meanwhile, reinvented itself as a global hub for finance, technology and creative industries — sectors that grew where the old ones declined.

Geography reinforces the gap. Most international flights and high-speed rail lines focus on London. Universities, headquarters and government departments cluster there. Better transport, more graduates and richer markets attract more firms, which create more jobs, which attract more workers — a self-reinforcing loop economists call a positive multiplier. Where this loop is missing, regions can fall into a negative multiplier — jobs leave, shops close, young people move away, the tax base shrinks, services are cut, and the next generation has even fewer reasons to stay.

Imagine a car factory opens in Sunderland. It hires 1,500 workers directly. Those workers spend money in local cafes, shops and gyms, supporting hundreds more jobs. Suppliers move in to be near the factory, hiring more staff. Taxes paid by all these workers fund schools, parks and roads. House prices firm up, attracting investment. The original 1,500 jobs end up supporting several thousand — that is the positive multiplier in action. Negative multipliers run the same loop in reverse when a major employer closes.

Consequences of Regional Inequality

An unbalanced economy creates real problems for everyone. London and the south-east struggle with overheating: house prices push young workers out, transport networks reach capacity, green belt land comes under pressure for housing. Northern regions struggle with the opposite: shrinking towns, empty shops, brain drain as graduates leave for southern jobs. Health, education and life expectancy gaps widen. Politically, divides like the 2016 EU referendum and 2019 general election highlighted very different priorities between regions.

Key Fact

A positive multiplier means new jobs, services and tax revenue feeding more growth. A negative multiplier means lost jobs leading to closed shops, falling tax revenue and people moving away. Both lock regions into self-reinforcing loops.

Trying to Rebalance the UK

Successive governments have tried to narrow the gap. Three approaches stand out. Infrastructure projects aim to plug northern cities into national networks: HS2, the proposed high-speed line from London to Birmingham (and originally to Manchester and Leeds), is the highest-profile example. Northern Powerhouse Rail and Crossrail upgrades aim to do the same.

Second, regeneration projects tackle specific places. Salford Quays in Greater Manchester turned derelict docks into MediaCityUK, attracting BBC studios and thousands of jobs. Liverpool’s Albert Dock has shifted from shipping to museums, housing and tourism. Cardiff Bay’s waterfront, once heavy industry, is now offices and apartments — a Welsh example of brownfield regeneration that anchors a positive multiplier.

Third, devolution gives more decision-making power to elected regional mayors and the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish governments. Newer policies like ‘levelling up’ aim to direct investment specifically to less-prosperous areas. Critics argue progress has been slow, and that new transport links can sometimes pull jobs towards London rather than away from it.

Many geographers argue that closing the divide also needs investment in skills, broadband, housing and creative industries — not just trains and roads. Moving public bodies out of London (Channel 4 to Leeds, the Treasury North in Darlington) signals where future jobs should grow. Targeted education funding, free port zones in coastal towns and small-business grants are also part of the toolkit. Closing a gap built up over 50 years is the work of a generation, not a single project.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark questions on UK regional inequalities, anchor every point in named places — Blackpool life expectancy, Salford Quays, HS2 — not just ‘the north’ or ‘the south’. For 8-mark evaluations, weigh the claim that one strategy alone can close the gap and reach a justified conclusion; markers want to see ‘On balance, infrastructure helps but only if combined with skills and devolution.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The UK’s north-south divide shows in GDP, life expectancy, unemployment and house prices, with London and the south-east leading and parts of the north, south Wales and northern Scotland trailing.
  • The divide grew from the collapse of heavy industry from the 1970s and is reinforced by positive multipliers in London and negative multipliers in declining regions.
  • Rebalancing strategies include infrastructure (HS2, Northern Powerhouse Rail), regeneration (Salford Quays, Cardiff Bay) and devolution to regional mayors and national governments.
